{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $v(x)={5}^{x}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot {5}^{x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot ({5}^{x})^{′}}{{({5}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot {5}^{x}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot {5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{{({5}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{5}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡5)}{{({5}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{{5}^{x}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f3ad1214-df3b-5446-bedc-f04cce151e2f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f3ad1214-df3b-5446-bedc-f04cce151e2f" :answer-field/id #uuid "f3ad1214-df3b-5446-bedc-f04cce151e2f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-b06ae33d-db5d-59f2-ab18-7eae753b3bbb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b06ae33d-db5d-59f2-ab18-7eae753b3bbb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b06ae33d-db5d-59f2-ab18-7eae753b3bbb" :answer/id #uuid "b06ae33d-db5d-59f2-ab18-7eae753b3bbb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\cos x-\ln(5)\sin x}{5^x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096622 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967" :question/id #uuid "11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967" :question/math-academy-id "q-340339" :question/problem "Given that $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{x}},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x}{{2}^{x}}\cdot ($
{{field-1}}
$).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={x}^{2}$ and $v={2}^{x}.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}\cdot 2x-{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{({2}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}\cdot x(2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}{{({2}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x(2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}{{2}^{x}} \\  & =\frac{x}{{2}^{x}}\cdot (\,2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/id #uuid "d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer/id #uuid "1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2-x\ln 2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097820 :tutorial/content "We know how to calculate the derivative of the product of two functions, but what if we have a quotient?

For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097822 :tutorial/content "We can now prove that $(\tan x)' = \sec^2{x}$ using the quotient rule. Here's how! 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096890 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172028 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/id #uuid "13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/math-academy-id "q-95398" :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=2.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=2
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2})-2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+2-2) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2}+2 & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}+\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}-{z}_{2}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the pair of intersecting lines ${z}_{2}=\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2}=-\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, adding $8$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-8 & \le 4 \\ -2x-8+8 & \le 4+8 \\ -2x+0 & \le 12 \\ -2x & \le 12\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x\,\, & \le \,\,12 \\ \frac{-2x}{-2}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{12}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}x}{\cancel{-2}}\, & \ge \,\,-6 \\ x\,\, & \ge \,-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -6.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3e6e9bff-56b9-56a9-abf2-3f9a586746de"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3e6e9bff-56b9-56a9-abf2-3f9a586746de" :answer-field/id #uuid "3e6e9bff-56b9-56a9-abf2-3f9a586746de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5984d0a1-af5a-506a-bd3d-f4742f93bd1e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c0d8ebb2-e776-553b-bcae-7b8cdfd081ce" "answer-5984d0a1-af5a-506a-bd3d-f4742f93bd1e" "answer-b1bb3fec-7fa5-56c4-bdbc-f9b4538f570f" "answer-ae2737bd-5a02-5f7d-b662-3be2c7a7a4b3" "answer-b8c556c6-37e1-5b77-8d76-57fcbc0b4c3f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c0d8ebb2-e776-553b-bcae-7b8cdfd081ce" :answer/id #uuid "c0d8ebb2-e776-553b-bcae-7b8cdfd081ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge -4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5984d0a1-af5a-506a-bd3d-f4742f93bd1e" :answer/id #uuid "5984d0a1-af5a-506a-bd3d-f4742f93bd1e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge -6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1bb3fec-7fa5-56c4-bdbc-f9b4538f570f" :answer/id #uuid "b1bb3fec-7fa5-56c4-bdbc-f9b4538f570f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge 2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae2737bd-5a02-5f7d-b662-3be2c7a7a4b3" :answer/id #uuid "ae2737bd-5a02-5f7d-b662-3be2c7a7a4b3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\le -4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b8c556c6-37e1-5b77-8d76-57fcbc0b4c3f" :answer/id #uuid "b8c556c6-37e1-5b77-8d76-57fcbc0b4c3f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\le -6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-24db3001-b38e-58e0-a2db-d37c5cfbbf6a" :question/id #uuid "24db3001-b38e-58e0-a2db-d37c5cfbbf6a" :question/math-academy-id "q-177678" :question/problem "The solution to the inequality $-10x-13<17$ is$\,x$

"0bcf3acb-d9f4-5535-b8d1-de8e7ee2e9d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-157235" :question/problem "Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $3{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=0.$

II. ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

III. The set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent." :question/worked-solution "We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3} & =3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 9 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -14 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6-4-2 \\ 9+5-14 \\ -3+3+0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since statement I is true, we have ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ for ${x}_{1}=3,\,{x}_{2}=-1$ and ${x}_{3}=2.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is false, the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly *dependent*.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24809e24-c6b5-5bd7-a31f-2f0864640659"] :db/ensure ["question-477025c6-a218-5107-ac1d-dc64cfa74878" :question/problem "Find where the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{4}-5$ at the point $(-1,-4)$ intersects the $x$-axis."] ["question-477025c6-a218-5107-ac1d-dc64cfa74878" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-5.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}-5)=4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m={f}^{′}(-1)=4(-1)^{3}=-4.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-4) & =-4(x+1) \\ y & =-4x-4-4 \\ y & =-4x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-4x-8 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(-2,0).$"] ["question-477025c6-a218-5107-ac1d-dc64cfa74878" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] The graph above shows that the volume of gas $L$ in a truck's tank is directly proportional to the time $t$ since the driver started filling it. Find a direct variation equation that describes the relationship between $L$ and $t.$"] ["question-eabcc9c8-1fae-5b8f-9d65-4f29f12ab5ce" :question/worked-solution "Since $L$ varies directly with $t,$ we use the equation

$$
L=kt.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $t=6$ and $L=90.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =k\cdot 6 \\ \frac{90}{6} & =k \\ 15 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
L=15t.
$$"] ["question-eabcc9c8-1fae-5b8f-9d65-4f29f12ab5ce" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bf78e6b5-1138-5983-a5e7-632caf3ecb6f" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{4}{3}
$$

Finally, we write the resulting improper fraction as a mixed number:

$$
\frac{4}{3}=1\,\text{R}1=1\,\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, the constant of proportionality is $1\,\frac{1}{3}$ dollars per pound."] ["question-d9eeaf2b-c92c-529e-9218-24a01a5754ee" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $u$ and $z.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?"] ["question-528c6dbc-6dbe-5499-88b0-b6881a756455" :question/worked-solution "Since $u$ varies directly with $z,$ we use the equation

$$
u=kz.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $z=-10$ and $u=2.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =k\cdot (-10) \\ -\frac{2}{10} & =k \\ -\frac{1}{5} & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
u=-\frac{1}{5}z.
$$"] ["question-528c6dbc-6dbe-5499-88b0-b6881a756455" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-35a7e094-9492-556b-b055-0b4284ba502d" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
2a-2b=2a+(-2b).
$$

- The vector $2a$ has the same direction as $a$ but twice the magnitude.

- The vector $-2b$ has the direction that is opposite to $b$ but twice the magnitude.

![](images/c1/c1cc845ddfe16f12169625e5f8404d3d92558b885ffde8c3ab02cdb2c096f699.png)

Now, we can draw $-2b$ starting from the head of $2a.$ The resultant 

$$
2a-2b
$$

goes from the tail of $2a$ to the head of $-2b.$

$$
-2p-4q
$$

goes from the tail of $-2p$ to the head of $-4q.$

:question/problem "Suppose we are given two vectors $a$ and $b$ where $a∦b.$ Find $\lambda$ and $\mu ,$ if 

$$
a-2b=(3\lambda -\mu )a-(\lambda -4\mu )b.
$$

$\lambda =$
{{field-1}}$,\,\mu =$
{{field-2}}"] ["question-d2a5cac6-33f2-5ce9-8655-67db2ef94b7e" :question/worked-solution "Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. So, the coefficients of $a$ must be equal, and the coefficients of $b$ must be equal.

Equating the coefficients, we get:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3\lambda -\mu &=1 \\ \lambda -4\mu &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\mu =3\lambda -1
$$

Substituting back into the second equation, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda -4\mu  & =2 \\ \lambda -4(3\lambda -1) & =2 \\ \lambda -12\lambda +4 & =2 \\ -11\lambda  & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\frac{2}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =3\lambda -1 \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{11}-1 \\  & =-\frac{5}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d2a5cac6-33f2-5ce9-8655-67db2ef94b7e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c60f15ed-8ce7-5564-85f4-7485ed35b513" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-d2a5cac6-33f2-5ce9-8655-67db2ef94b7e"] [17592186096970 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186097835 :tutorial/content "A **linear combination** of two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is a sum of multiples of the two vectors. 

For example, let's consider the vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b,$ shown below:

![](images/00/0091edb7bcd026737e7bdf9d56e5a9932970d62902a185f76599cdf18bfd9d45.png)

One particular linear combination of these vectors is 

$$
2 \mathbf{a} + 3 \mathbf{b} = 2 \cdot \mathbf{a} + 3 \cdot \mathbf{b}.
$$

If we draw this linear combination in the coordinate plane, we get the following:

![](images/73/73a73b7e90c9e82e57f88d04079a69fa2cce082fc6d7f4667fae1cb4190ea46a.png)"] [17592186097836 :tutorial/content "If two vectors are not parallel, then each linear combination can only be written in one way. 

For example, if we have two vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ and two real numbers $\alpha,\beta,$ then the equality

$$
2 \mathbf{a} + 3 \mathbf{b} = \alpha \mathbf{a} + \beta \mathbf{b}
$$

holds if and only if $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=3$.

In other words, the pair of numbers $\alpha,\beta$ defines a unique vector $\alpha \mathbf{a} + \beta \mathbf{b}.$ That is to say, if

$$
\alpha_1 \mathbf{a} + \beta_1 \mathbf{b} = \alpha_2 \mathbf{a} + \beta_2 \mathbf{b},
$$

then $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2$ and $\beta_1 = \beta_2.$

**Watch out!** This property holds only if two vectors *are not parallel*."] [17592186096885 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0] ["question-7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342" :question/id #uuid "7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342"] ["question-7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342" :question/math-academy-id "q-42470"] ["question-7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342" :question/problem "Find $6det(A)-2det(B)$, where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ \sqrt{3} & 1 & 2 & 9 \\ 1 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} & 3 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$"] ["question-7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each matrix in turn.

- Since $A$ has two identical rows, we obtain

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ \sqrt{3} & 1 & 2 & 9 \\ 1 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,det(A)=0.
$$

- Since $B$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, its determinant is:

$$
det(B)=3\sqrt{2}\cdot 0-1\cdot 3=-3
$$

Therefore, $6det(A)-2det(B)=6\cdot 0-2\cdot (-3)=6.$"] ["question-7fe1aa9d-37dc-5179-a9aa-2b200892c342" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+2}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+3}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero."] ["question-0d6ccda5-f064-5d51-bbf4-385a52f598a9" :question/id #uuid "0d6ccda5-f064-5d51-bbf4-385a52f598a9"] ["question-0d6ccda5-f064-5d51-bbf4-385a52f598a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-28194"] ["question-0d6ccda5-f064-5d51-bbf4-385a52f598a9" :question/problem "Given that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-4x-2,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)"] ["question-0d6ccda5-f064-5d51-bbf4-385a52f598a9" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -1 & -1 & -3 & -4 & -2 \\  &  & 1 & 2 & 2 \\  & -1 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+1} & =-{x}^{2}-2x-2 \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x+2),\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}+2x+2=0$ is 

$$
D={2}^{2}-4(1)(2)=-4<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-1.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
y=-(0)^{3}-3(0)^{2}-4(0)-2=-2
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-2),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,3),$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{9{x}^{3}-4x}{3{x}^{2}+2x} & =\frac{9(0)^{3}-4(0)}{3(0)^{2}+2(0)}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9{x}^{3}-4x}{3{x}^{2}+2x} & =\frac{x(9{x}^{2}-4)}{x(3x+2)} \\  & =\frac{9{x}^{2}-4}{3x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{9{x}^{3}-4x}{3{x}^{2}+2x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{9{x}^{2}-4}{3x+2} \\  & =\frac{0-4}{0+2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f8c786dd-8e95-5f38-8555-c19baa5a85a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5de46a5c-045a-5a65-93fe-1ee8641452b2" :answer-field/id #uuid \begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-3}{{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{(-1)^{2}-2(-1)-3}{(-1)^{2}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-3}{{x}^{2}-1} & =\frac{(x+1)(x-3)}{(x-1)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{x-3}{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-3}{{x}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{x-3}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{-1-3}{-1-1} \\  & =\frac{-4}{-2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{{y}^{3}-9y}{{y}^{2}-5y+6} & =\frac{{3}^{3}-9(3)}{{3}^{2}-5(3)+6}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{3}-9y}{{y}^{2}-5y+6} & =\frac{y({y}^{2}-9)}{(y-2)(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{y(y-3)(y+3)}{(y-2)(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{y(y+3)}{(y-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{{y}^{3}-9y}{{y}^{2}-5y+6} & ={lim}_{y\to 3}\frac{y(y+3)}{y-2} \\  & =\frac{3(3+3)}{3-2} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7acf7423-e8b7-5b28-a3d4-100be04f8153" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8d7ede5a-d5a6-5e6e-9812-54ef505e6966" :answer-field/id #uuid The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(x-5) & =2 \\ {3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x-5)} & ={3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x-5)}=x-5.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & ={3}^{2} \\ x-5 & =9 \\ x & =14.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1eda43e3-b2a8-5d39-8cf8-7675e676743f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8b5d6150-ecf7-5f47-90e3-e6ef4745bb15" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-2f3b2436-4186-5dc4-8dde-9327a375de0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-79388"] ["question-2f3b2436-4186-5dc4-8dde-9327a375de0e" :question/problem "If $7{log}_{5}⁡x-2{log}_{5}⁡x=10$, then what is the value of  $x?$"] ["question-2f3b2436-4186-5dc4-8dde-9327a375de0e" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{log}_{5}⁡x-2{log}_{5}⁡x & =10 \\ (7-2){log}_{5}⁡x & =10 \\ 5{log}_{5}⁡x & =10 \\ {log}_{5}⁡x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $5,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡x & =2 \\ {5}^{{log}_{5}⁡x} & ={5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${5}^{{log}_{5}⁡x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={5}^{2} \\ x & =25.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2f3b2436-4186-5dc4-8dde-9327a375de0e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d37a1738-f25e-5f6b-a20f-5e8e1491c6e4" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-eb08b876-0b66-567e-a3b3-60f7e35a27a7" :question/problem "Which of the following are logically equivalent to $M?$

I. $(M∧L)∧M$

II. $M∧(M∨L)$

III. $(L∨M)∧M$"] ["question-eb08b876-0b66-567e-a3b3-60f7e35a27a7" :question/worked-solution "The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as

$$
M∧(M∨L)≡M.
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is *not*  logically equivalent to $M.$
This statement cannot be simplified using the absorption laws.

- Statement II is logically equivalent to $M.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M∧(M∨L) & ≡M.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is logically equivalent to $M.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(L∨M)∧M & ≡M∧(L∨M) \\  & ≡M∧(M∨L) \\  & ≡M.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-eb08b876-0b66-567e-a3b3-60f7e35a27a7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] expressions.

- The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as

$$
A \land (A \lor B) \equiv A.
$$

- Likewise, the law that disjunction absorbs conjunction is stated as

$$
A \lor (A \land B) \equiv A.
$$

Sometimes, the laws are stated more concisely as

$$
A \land (A \lor B) \equiv A \lor (A \land B) \equiv A.
$$

$$

$$

Consequently, $c=\frac{4}{3}a+\lambda b=\frac{4}{3}a+\frac{1}{4}b.$

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =2b+a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a+2b=a+2b.$

["question-f860d929-2f10-587c-a6b0-b33c9769a489" :question/problem "Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=(3-x)(1-x)^{2}?$"] ["question-f860d929-2f10-587c-a6b0-b33c9769a489" :question/worked-solution "The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=3$ and a double root at $x=1.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(3-0)(1-0)^{2} \\  & =(3)(1)^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,3),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=1.$

Notice that the leading coefficient is *negative*:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(3-x)(1-x)^{2} \\  & =(3-x)({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =-{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-75163"] ["question-024af745-75a4-59f6-8f6d-ac762eef1195" :question/problem "Given that $x+3$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}-15x-9$, which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

*(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)*"] ["question-024af745-75a4-59f6-8f6d-ac762eef1195" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & -1 & -7 & -15 & -9 \\  &  & 3 & 12 & 9 \\  & -1 & -4 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+3} & =-{x}^{2}-4x-3 \\  & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x+3)({x}^{2}+4x+3).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=-(x+3)(x+1)(x+3)=-(x+1)(x+3)^{2}
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-1$ and a double root at $x=-3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0+1)(0+3)^{2} \\  & =-(1)(3)^{2} \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-9),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-3.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{5x+16}-3=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[4]{5x+16}-3 & =0 \\ \sqrt[4]{5x+16} & =3 \\ (\sqrt[4]{5x+16})^{4} & ={3}^{4} \\ 5x+16 & =81 \\ 5x & =65 \\ x & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we must check the answer by substituting it back into the initial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[4]{5\cdot 13+16}-3 & =0 \\ \sqrt[4]{81}-3 & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/bd/bd1d4466a6a0d7f8640200c999170dff2aa2762fc2cd14a8e61c110c6e94b189.png)

Using the given information and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =10 \\ f(1) & =f(-3)+{\int }_{-3}^{1}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =10-5 \\  & =5 \\ f(3) & =f(-3)+{\int }_{-3}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =10+(-5+2) \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the largest value of $f$ from our candidates. 

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
{f}_{\text{max}}=max\{10,5,7\}=10.
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is ${f}_{\text{max}}=10,$ and the value of $x$ that maximizes $f(x)$ is ${x}_{\text{max}}=-3.$"] ["question-63b0fa41-9cba-5e63-9815-21bb52243039" ["question-1f4665bd-3b2f-5e28-98c1-a2915a1c6960" :question/worked-solution "First, we subtract and add $7$ in the numerator. This reveals a copy of the denominator without changing the value of the expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x-1}{4x-7} &=\frac{4x-7+7-1}{4x-7}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we split the fraction into two, and then simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x-7+7-1}{4x-7} & =\frac{4x-7}{4x-7}+\frac{7-1}{4x-7} \\  & =1+\frac{6}{4x-7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $a=1$ and $b=6,$ and we get

$$
a+b=1+6=7.
$$"] ["question-1f4665bd-3b2f-5e28-98c1-a2915a1c6960" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0b37f42c-dcbd-5572-b8fc-d3cf6928d353" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Then, we split the fraction into two, and then simplify:

$V=${{field-1}}"] ["question-443a4021-2ecb-5b8a-948d-b71804528fab" :question/worked-solution "The volume of a parallelepiped spanned by three vectors is given by the absolute value of their triple product.

First, we compute the triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix}-0\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+5\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(2\cdot 1-6\cdot 4)+0+5(3\cdot 4-2\cdot 0) \\  & =-22+60 \\  & =38\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the absolute value. So, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped is 

$$

$$"] ["question-443a4021-2ecb-5b8a-948d-b71804528fab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db" :answer-field/id #uuid "2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db"] ["answer-ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213" :answer/id #uuid "ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213"] ["answer-ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213" :answer/value "38"] ["answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db" :answer-field/correct "answer-ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213"] ["answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db" :answer-field/choices "answer-ad103bee-c9bb-538f-b95a-de0c98d63213"] ["question-443a4021-2ecb-5b8a-948d-b71804528fab" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-2566d49a-718e-5a8c-9b71-cc6e6ef2e3db"] [17592186105907 :knowledge-point/questions "question-443a4021-2ecb-5b8a-948d-b71804528fab"] ["question-c885246f-c4a6-5da3-b8cb-28ee3dc779d8" :question/id #uuid "c885246f-c4a6-5da3-b8cb-28ee3dc779d8"] ["question-c885246f-c4a6-5da3-b8cb-28ee3dc779d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-280713"] ["question-c885246f-c4a6-5da3-b8cb-28ee3dc779d8" :question/problem "Compute the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors $x=⟨2,3,0⟩$, $y=⟨1,4,5⟩$, and $z=⟨0,2,6⟩.$

First, we compute the triple product:

$$

$$

$k=${{field-1}}"] ["question-ef51444c-d286-591b-9ba9-aedca70d62d8" :question/worked-solution "Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =\begin{vmatrix}k & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =k\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5\end{vmatrix}-k\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =k(3\cdot 5-0\cdot 4)-k(1\cdot 5-0\cdot 0)+2(1\cdot 4-3\cdot 0) \\  & =k(15)-k(5)+2(4) \\  & =15k-5k+8 \\  & =10k+8\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 10k+8 & =0 \\ 10k & =-8 \\ k & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{4}{5}.$"] ["question-ef51444c-d286-591b-9ba9-aedca70d62d8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b" :answer-field/id #uuid "2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b"] ["answer-efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7" :answer/id #uuid "efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7"] ["answer-efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7" :answer/value "-\frac{4}{5}"] ["answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b" :answer-field/correct "answer-efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7"] ["answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b" :answer-field/choices "answer-efac262e-978f-52d8-b514-d218c8e2aaf7"] ["question-ef51444c-d286-591b-9ba9-aedca70d62d8" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-2170e711-c9bf-56cc-a436-de505690692b"] [17592186105908 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ef51444c-d286-591b-9ba9-aedca70d62d8"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/id #uuid "02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/math-academy-id "q-280320"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/problem "Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(0,2,-1),$ $B(3,4,1),$ $C(-1,3,2),$ and $D(2,1,0).$

$V=${{field-1}}"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(3i+4j+k)-(2j-k) \\  & =3i+2j+2k \\  & =⟨3,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(-i+3j+2k)-(2j-k) \\  & =-i+j+3k \\  & =⟨-1,1,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(2i+j)-(2j-k) \\  & =2i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(1\cdot 1-3\cdot (-1))-2((-1)\cdot 1-3\cdot 2)+2((-1)\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 2) \\  & =3(1+3)-2(-1-6)+2(1-2) \\  & =12-(-14)-2 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelpiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|24|=24.
$$"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2" :answer-field/id #uuid "752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2"] ["answer-bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375" :answer/id #uuid "bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375"] ["answer-bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375" :answer/value "24"] ["answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2" :answer-field/correct "answer-bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375"] ["answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2" :answer-field/choices "answer-bd4b21f5-ae4e-533c-a49c-e215e4954375"] ["question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-752eecbd-7383-564b-9c0e-74b4d04c57f2"] [17592186105909 :knowledge-point/questions "question-02e4dd76-291f-501d-9dd9-df687e45b52b"] ["question-7e38002f-06be-5b6a-8718-39abfb36add8" :question/id #uuid "7e38002f-06be-5b6a-8718-39abfb36add8"] ["question-7e38002f-06be-5b6a-8718-39abfb36add8" :question/math-academy-id "q-71022"] ["question-7e38002f-06be-5b6a-8718-39abfb36add8" :question/problem "Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-t \\ y &=-3-2t \\ z &=4+7t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line."] ["question-7e38002f-06be-5b6a-8718-39abfb36add8" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-t \\ -3-2t \\ 4+7t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-t \\ -2t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(0,-3,4)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-1,-2,7⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-3)}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{7}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$

:question/problem "Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ 7\end{bmatrix},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$"] ["question-3f6ecd28-8af0-5770-801c-e2211846f047" :question/worked-solution "Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{0}=\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{0}=\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1:$

$$
r=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2+5t \\ 4+7t\end{bmatrix},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1$, as follows:

$$
\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7},\,x=-1
$$"] ["question-3f6ecd28-8af0-5770-801c-e2211846f047" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b7fb6b07-3aa3-5e0b-beb1-701386482c7a" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-17245a50-7006-5425-919f-edc58b5da5cf" :question/worked-solution "The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=1-{x}^{2},$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (1-{x}^{2})-x\cdot (-2x)}{{(1-{x}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}}{{(1-{x}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{{(1-{x}^{2})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-17245a50-7006-5425-919f-edc58b5da5cf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847" :answer-field/id #uuid "1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847"] ["answer-5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484" :answer/id #uuid "5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484"] ["answer-5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484" :answer/value "\frac{1+x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}"] ["answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847" :answer-field/correct "answer-5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484"] ["answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847" :answer-field/choices "answer-5bfe7a9c-764b-5756-917f-0f8851387484"] ["question-17245a50-7006-5425-919f-edc58b5da5cf" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-1b10a7e0-6602-5d46-9e5d-83b14c5c8847"] [17592186096620 :knowledge-point/questions "question-17245a50-7006-5425-919f-edc58b5da5cf"] ["question-e77736b2-0ba9-5e43-b9dd-36b855b6cec7" :question/id #uuid "e77736b2-0ba9-5e43-b9dd-36b855b6cec7"] ["question-e77736b2-0ba9-5e43-b9dd-36b855b6cec7" :question/math-academy-id "q-11964"] ["question-e77736b2-0ba9-5e43-b9dd-36b855b6cec7" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\frac{5{x}^{2}}{9x-7}$, find ${f}^{′}(x).$"] ["question-e77736b2-0ba9-5e43-b9dd-36b855b6cec7" :question/worked-solution "The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=5{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=9x-7,$ respectively. $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x}{{2}^{x}}\cdot ($

$).$"] ["question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={x}^{2}$ and $v={2}^{x}.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}\cdot 2x-{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{({2}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}\cdot x(2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}{{({2}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x(2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}{{2}^{x}} \\  & =\frac{x}{{2}^{x}}\cdot (\,2-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/id #uuid "d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c"] ["answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer/id #uuid "1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d"] ["answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d" :answer/value "2-x\ln 2"] ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/correct "answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d"] ["answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c" :answer-field/choices "answer-1b8e10fe-6e80-5383-bdd4-03771b7b677d"] ["question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-d98c469b-477b-57e5-af28-2ff378fcb14c"] [17592186096622 :knowledge-point/questions "question-11dd8eeb-96f6-50fa-a820-1e22e1912967"] [17592186097820 :tutorial/content "We know how to calculate the derivative of the product of two functions, but what if we have a quotient?

For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186097822 :tutorial/content "We can now prove that $(\tan x)' = \sec^2{x}$ using the quotient rule. Here's how! 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186096890 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/id #uuid "13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393"] ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/math-academy-id "q-95398"] ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=2.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$"] ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=2
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2})-2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+2-2) & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2}+2 & =2 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}+\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}+\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}-{z}_{2}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the pair of intersecting lines ${z}_{2}=\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2}=-\sqrt{3}{z}_{1}.$"] ["question-13426e81-09a1-5f21-879b-4654e3684393" :question/difficulty ["question-0bcf3acb-d9f4-5535-b8d1-de8e7ee2e9d3" :question/problem "Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $3{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=0.$

II. ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

III. The set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent."] ["question-0bcf3acb-d9f4-5535-b8d1-de8e7ee2e9d3" :question/worked-solution "We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3} & =3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 9 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -14 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6-4-2 \\ 9+5-14 \\ -3+3+0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since statement I is true, we have ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ for ${x}_{1}=3,\,{x}_{2}=-1$ and ${x}_{3}=2.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is false, the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly *dependent*.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-0bcf3acb-d9f4-5535-b8d1-de8e7ee2e9d3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] vectors.

For example, let's consider the vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, shown below:

![](images/00/0091edb7bcd026737e7bdf9d56e5a9932970d62902a185f76599cdf18bfd9d45.png)

One particular linear combination of these vectors is

$$
2 \mathbf{a} + 3 \mathbf{b} = 2 \cdot \mathbf{a} + 3 \cdot \mathbf{b}
$$

If we draw this linear combination in the coordinate plane, we get the following:

![](images/73/73a73b7e90c9e82e57f88d04079a69fa2cce082fc6d7f4667fae1cb4190ea46a.png)"] [17592186097836 :tutorial/content "If two vectors are not parallel, then each linear combination can only be written in one way.

For example, if we have two vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b}$, and two real numbers $\alpha,\beta$, then the equality

$$
2 \mathbf{a} + 3 \mathbf{b} = \alpha \mathbf{a} + \beta \mathbf{b}
$$

holds if and only if $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=3$.

In other words, the pair of numbers $\alpha,\beta$ defines a unique vector $\alpha \mathbf{a} + \beta \mathbf{b}$. That is to say, if

$$
\alpha_1 \mathbf{a} + \beta_1 \mathbf{b} = \alpha_2 \mathbf{a} + \beta_2 \mathbf{b}
$$

then

$$
\alpha_1 = \alpha_2
$$

and

$$
\beta_1 = \beta_2
$$

**Watch out!** This property holds only if two vectors *are not parallel*."] [17592186135151 :tutorial/content "If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+2}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+3}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}| \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero."] [17592186158576 :tutorial/content "The **associative law for conjunctions** states that when we have multiple conjunctions in a row, the placement of parentheses does not matter:

is logically equivalent to the sentence

$$\underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{The dog is loud}}_{(B} \quad \underbrace{\textrm{or}\vphantom{p}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{the cat is quiet}}_{A)}.$$"] [17592186158482 :tutorial/content "There are two laws, called the **absorption laws**, that can be used to drastically simplify some logical expressions.

- The law that conjunction absorbs disjunction is stated as $$A \land (A \lor B) \equiv A.$$
- Likewise, the law that disjunction absorbs conjunction is stated as $$A \lor (A \land B) \equiv A.$$

Sometimes, the laws are stated more concisely as

$$A \land (A \lor B) \equiv A \lor (A \land B) \equiv A.$$

To prove that these laws hold, we can construct truth tables:

| $\color{blue} \textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{blue} \textrm F$ | $\color{blue} \textrm F$ |"] [17592186097820 :tutorial/content "We know how to calculate the derivative of the product of two functions, but what if we have a quotient?

For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =(x)^{'}=1, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{'}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186097822 :tutorial/content "We can now prove that $(\tan x)' = \sec^2{x}$ using the quotient rule. Here's how!

:topic/math-academy-id 1947} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** \n\nThe procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:\n\n*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.\n\nLet's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\\{(x,y)\\in \\mathbb R^2: \\,  x^2 +y^2  \\leq 1\\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?\n\nTo find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:\n\n**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$\n\n![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)\n\nTo determine the critical points, we solve $\\boldsymbol f' = \\mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives\n\n![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)\n\nThe derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\{\\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0 \\\\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}x=0 \\\\ y=0.\\end{aligned}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\langle \\cos{t}, \\sin{t} \\rangle, \\qquad t \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \\in (0,2\\pi),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ ({e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\\\ -2\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis equation has three solutions, namely \n\n$$\nt =\\dfrac\\pi 2, \\: \\pi, \\: \\dfrac{3\\pi}2 \\in (0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are \n\n$$\nt=0, \\: \\dfrac{\\pi}{2}, \\:  \\pi, \\: \\dfrac{3\\pi}{2}.\n$$\n\nEvaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:\n\n$$\n(1,0), \\: (0,1), \\: (-1,0), \\: (0,-1)\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.\n\nEvaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:\n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \\, (0,-1),$ and\n\n- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \\, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124737} {:db/id 17592186125655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** \n\nThe procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:\n\n*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.\n\nLet's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\\{(x,y)\\in \\mathbb R^2: \\,  x^2 +y^2  \\leq 1\\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?\n\nTo find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:\n\n**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$\n\n![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)\n\nTo determine the critical points, we solve $\\boldsymbol f' = \\mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives\n\n![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)\n\nThe derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\{\\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0 \\\\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}x=0 \\\\ y=0.\\end{aligned}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{r} = \\langle \\cos{t}, \\sin{t} \\rangle, \\qquad t \\in [0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \\in (0,2\\pi),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ ({e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\\\ -2\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis equation has three solutions, namely \n\n$$\nt =\\dfrac\\pi 2, \\: \\pi, \\: \\dfrac{3\\pi}2 \\in (0,2\\pi).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are \n\n$$\nt=0, \\: \\dfrac{\\pi}{2}, \\:  \\pi, \\: \\dfrac{3\\pi}{2}.\n$$\n\nEvaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:\n\n$$\n(1,0), \\: (0,1), \\: (-1,0), \\: (0,-1)\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.\n\nEvaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:\n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \\, (0,-1),$ and\n\n- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \\, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id $(-2,-4),$ $(-1,-1),$ $(1,-1),$ and $(2,-4).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on global extrema for $f.$ These are\n\n$$\n(-2,-4),\\,(-1,-1),\\,(1,-1),\\,(2,-4).\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. \n\nEvaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(0,-3) & =2(0)(-3)+6(0)-3 \\\\  & =-3 \\\\ f(-2,-4) & =2(-2)(-4)+6(-2)-3 \\\\  & =1 \\\\ f(-1,-1) & =2(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-3 \\\\  & =-7 \\\\ f(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)+6(1)-3 \\\\  & =1 \\\\ f(2,-4) & =2(2)(-4)+6(2)-3 \\\\  & =-7\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-7$ at the points $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,-4),$\n\n- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(-2,-4)$ and $(1,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives\n\n$$\nr=⟨\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\\,t\\in [0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =(\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\\\  & =3+2\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\\in (0,2\\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ (3+2\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\\\ 2\\sqrt{3}\\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis equation gives two solutions $t=\\frac{\\pi }{2},\\frac{3\\pi }{2}\\in (0,2\\pi ).$\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\\\  & =0+1-2 \\\\  & =-1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ &=0 \\\\ -4x &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\\\ y &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0)\\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives\n\n$$\nr=⟨3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,\\frac{3}{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\\,t\\in [0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,\\frac{3}{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =1-4(3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\\frac{3}{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =1-18\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\\\  & =1-9\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\\in (0,2\\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ (1-9\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\\\ -18\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe final equation gives four solutions, namely\n\n$$\nt=\\frac{\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{5\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{7\\pi }{4}\\in (0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. \n\nEvaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: \n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(3,0)$ gives\n\n$$\n{f}^{′}(x,y)=\\begin{bmatrix}-4y,\\,-4x\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nThe derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-4y &=0 \\\\ -4x &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\\\ y &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0)\\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives\n\n$$\nr=⟨3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\\,\\frac{3}{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\\,t\\in [0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the =1-4(3\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\\frac{3}{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =1-18\\operatorname{cos}⁡t\\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\\\  & =1-9\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\\in (0,2\\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ (1-9\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\\\ -18\\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe final equation gives four solutions, namely\n\n$$\nt=\\frac{\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{5\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{7\\pi }{4}\\in (0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are \n\n$$\nt=0,\\,\\frac{\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{5\\pi }{4},\\,\\frac{7\\pi }{4}.\n$$\n\nEvaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. \n\nEvaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: \n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(3,0)$ Computing the derivative gives\n\n$$\n{f}^{′}(x,y)=\\begin{bmatrix}-2x,\\,2y\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nThe derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-2x &=0 \\\\ 2y &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\\\ y &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0)\\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives\n\n$$\nr=⟨4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\\,t\\in [0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =1-(4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\\\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\\\  & =1-16\\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\\in (0,2\\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ (1-16\\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\\\ 32\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe final equation gives four solutions, namely\n\n$$\nt=\\frac{\\pi }{2},\\,\\pi ,\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{2}\\in (0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are \n\n$$\nt=0,\\,\\frac{\\pi }{2},\\,\\pi ,\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{2}.\n$$\n\nEvaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:\n\n$$\n(4,0),\\,(0,4),\\,(-4,0),\\,(0,-4)\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. \n\nEvaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: \n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and Computing the derivative gives\n\n$$\n{f}^{′}(x,y)=\\begin{bmatrix}-2x,\\,2y\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nThe derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-2x &=0 \\\\ 2y &=0\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⟹\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\\\ y &=0.\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives us a single point $(0,0)\\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.\n\n**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. \n\nTo find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives\n\n$$\nr=⟨4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\\,t\\in [0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nThe values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\\\  & =f(4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\\\  & =1-(4\\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\\\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\\\  & =1-16\\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\\in (0,2\\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\\\ (1-16\\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\\\ 32\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe final equation gives four solutions, namely\n\n$$\nt=\\frac{\\pi }{2},\\,\\pi ,\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{2}\\in (0,2\\pi ).\n$$\n\nWe also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are \n\n$$\nt=0,\\,\\frac{\\pi }{2},\\,\\pi ,\\,\\frac{3\\pi }{2}.\n$$\n\nEvaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:\n\n$$\n(4,0),\\,(0,4),\\,(-4,0),\\,(0,-4)\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. \n\nEvaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: \n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |\n\nTherefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that \n\n- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and "Find where the tangent to the curve $y=\\frac{2}{x}+x$ at the point  $(2,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.\n\nThe tangent intersects the $x$-axis at\n$($\n{{field-1}}$,$\n{{field-2}} $).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=\\frac{2}{x}+x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{2}{x}+x) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{2}{x})+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(x) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-1})+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(x) \\\\  & =-2{x}^{-2}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the slope of the tangent at our point is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(2) \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{{2}^{2}}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{4}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{2}+1 \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation of the tangent is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\\\ y-3 & =\\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\\\ y & =\\frac{1}{2}x-1+3 \\\\ y & =\\frac{1}{2}x+2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{2}x+2 & =0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{2}x & =-2 \\\\ x & =-2\\cdot 2 \\\\ x & =-4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the point of intersection is $(-4,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186547002 :question/id #uuid is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(-1)=5(-1)^{4}=5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation of the tangent is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\\\ y-1 & =5(x+1) \\\\ y & =5x+5+1 \\\\ y & =5x+6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}0 & =5x+6 \\\\ x & =-\\frac{6}{5}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the point of intersection is $(-\\frac{6}{5},0).$"} {:db/id 17592186049119} {:db/id 17592186049248} {:db/id 17592186050420} {:db/id 17592186051084} \n\nFinally, we substitute the slope $m=2$ and the coordinates of $P(1,1)$ into the point-slope form, and get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-1 & =2(x-1) \\\\ y & =2x-2+1 \\\\ y & :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)={x}^{5}+2.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}({x}^{5}+2)=5{x}^{4}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the slope of the tangent at our point is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(-1)=5(-1)^{4}=5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation of the tangent is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\\\ y-1 & =5(x+1) \\\\ y & =5x+5+1 \\\\ y & =5x+6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}0 & =5x+6 \\\\ x & =-\\frac{6}{5}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the point of intersection is $(-\\frac{6}{5},0).$"} :step/id #uuid "8f0e1de1-445c-5ef0-8ebc-283d32ff2db4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547140}} :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=\\frac{2}{x}+x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{2}{x}+x) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\frac{2}{x})+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(x) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-1})+\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(x) \\\\  & =-2{x}^{-2}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the slope of the tangent at our point is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(2) \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{{2}^{2}}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{4}+1 \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{2}+1 \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation of the tangent is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\\\ y-3 & =\\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\\\ y & =\\frac{1}{2}x-1+3 \\\\ y & =\\frac{1}{2}x+2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{2}x+2 & =0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{2}x & =-2 \\\\ x & =-2\\cdot 2 \\\\ x & =-4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the point of intersection is $(-4,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "b17b54ae-3884-5315-bfe6-1b6dd906db79"}] :activity/title :step/content {:db/id 17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \\times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z=9 \\\\ 2y+3z=7 \\\\ -8x+y+6z=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFirst, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z=9 \\\\ 0x+2y+3z=7 \\\\ then its determinant is equal to zero.\n\nFor example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:\n\n![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)\n\nThe second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\\ast$) may represent any number.\n\nLet's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+2}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+3}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =0+0+0 \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "cee0a552-60f2-5785-a506-63bd053364c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b68428f5-f5bb-5090-b7f9-4971dc931914" :step/math-academy-id 41745 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134902}} {:db/id 17592186134902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135152 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:\n\n![](images/74/7477781b618ec384b1638d01707acf545e7d9882ffca5bbc0efde4e224b04308.svg)\n\nWe can subtract the $1$st row from the $3$rd row, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 1\\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =B\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\\det(A) = \\det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\det(A) = \\det(B) = 0.\n$$\n\nNotice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:\n\n*If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "6813d49e-3908-5735-8196-8e1aad5a14e6"
